name: SchroederTrader
paragraph: SchroederTrader is an AI-driven stock trading system currently in Phase 1, implementing a rule-based SMA crossover strategy for SPY trading against Alpaca's paper trading API. The system uses a modular pipeline architecture spanning data ingestion, signal generation, risk management, order execution, trade logging, and email alerts, with each component cleanly separated (e.g., `strategy/sma_crossover.py` for 50/200 SMA signals, `risk/risk_manager.py` for position sizing, `storage/trade_log.py` for SQLite persistence). Notable technical choices include using `uv` for dependency management and Python 3.12+, persisting state as CSV files committed back to the repository, and leveraging GitHub Actions with timezone-aware cron scheduling (separate entries for EDT/EST) to run the bot daily at market close (4:30 PM ET Monday–Friday). The codebase is actively maintained with 273 commits and appears production-oriented, integrating both broker APIs (Alpaca) and LLM services (Anthropic, OpenAI) as secrets, suggesting exploration beyond the current rule-based phase. The repository is well-documented with setup instructions, a clear architectural table, and backtest infrastructure for strategy validation before live deployment.

# SchroederTrader

AI-driven stock trading system. Currently in **Phase 1**: rule-based SMA crossover bot for SPY.

## Quick Start

### Prerequisites
- Python 3.12+
- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)
- [Alpaca](https://app.alpaca.markets) paper trading account
- Gmail account with [app password](https://myaccount.google.com/apppasswords)

### Setup

```bash
# Clone and enter project
git clone https://github.com/dads2busy/SchroederTrader.git
cd SchroederTrader

# Create environment and install dependencies
uv venv
uv pip install -e ".[dev,backtest]"

# Configure credentials
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env with your Alpaca API keys and Gmail app password

# Run backtest
uv run python backtest/download_data.py
uv run python backtest/run_backtest.py

# Test the pipeline
uv run pytest tests/ -v

# Install cron job (runs daily at 4:30 PM ET)
./scripts/setup_cron.sh
```

## Architecture

Modular pipeline: data → strategy → risk → execution → storage → alerts

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `data/market_data.py` | Fetch OHLCV bars from Alpaca |
| `strategy/sma_crossover.py` | 50/200 SMA crossover signal generation |
| `risk/risk_manager.py` | Position sizing and guards |
| `execution/broker.py` | Order submission via Alpaca |
| `storage/trade_log.py` | SQLite trade logging |
| `alerts/email_alert.py` | Gmail notifications |

## Running on GitHub Actions

State is persisted as CSV files under `data/` and committed back to the repo
on each run. The workflow at `.github/workflows/daily.yml` fires Mon-Fri at
16:30 ET (two cron entries cover EDT/EST).

### Required repository secrets

Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret:

| Name | Value |

| `ALPACA_API_KEY` | Alpaca paper API key |
| `ALPACA_SECRET_KEY` | Alpaca paper API secret |

| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Anthropic API key |

name: proposer
paragraph: Proposer is a Python tooling suite that assists researchers in drafting grant proposals by automating three distinct pre-writing tasks: extracting structural requirements and section instructions from official funding solicitations (NOFOs/FOAs), identifying and ranking relevant senior personnel from a curated researcher corpus, and conducting directed adversarial literature reviews based on candidate research directions. Each tool produces human-readable artifacts meant to scaffold the drafting process rather than generate final text, feeding downstream into a separate proposal-reviewer tool that scores completed drafts for compliance. The project is in early design stage with no production function code yet, as evidenced by a recent design specification dated July 2026. A key technical choice is backend flexibility—all three functions can execute against either local models via Ollama or cloud-based models through Anthropic, selectable per invocation while maintaining network-based data retrieval for solicitations, literature, and publication records regardless of inference backend. The architecture is modular, with personnel matching sourcing from a separate research-corpus repository that generalizes a single-subject profile pipeline into a multi-subject system, suggesting Aaron designed proposer as part of a larger ecosystem of proposal-related tooling.
readme_excerpt:
# proposer

Pre-drafting assistance for research proposals. Three independent tools that run
*before* [`proposal-reviewer`](../proposal-reviewer), each producing an artifact a
human uses while preparing a proposal:

- **F1 — Structure** (`proposer structure`): extract the required proposal skeleton
  and per-section instructions from an official solicitation (NOFO/FOA).
- **F2 — Personnel** (`proposer personnel`): a recall aid for a research
  administrator assembling a team — which senior personnel to consider for each
  section, drawn from a curated corpus of researcher profiles.
- **F3 — Literature review** (`proposer litreview`): given candidate research
  direction(s) from the researcher, run a directed, adversarial literature review.

These are aids, not oracles. A human drafts using their output; the draft is then
scored by `proposal-reviewer`.

## Status

**Early design.** See [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-16-proposer-design.md`](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-16-proposer-design.md)
for the design in progress. No function code yet.

## Companion repos

- `proposal-reviewer` — offline compliance scorer for a finished draft (the tool
  these three feed into).
- `research-corpus` — the persistent, curated corpus of senior-personnel profiles
  that F2 reads (a separate repo; generalizes the `dads2busy.github.io` profile
  pipeline from one subject to many).

## Model backends

Each function can run on a **local** (Ollama) or **cloud** (Anthropic) model,
selectable per run (`--backend {local,cloud}`) with sensible per-function defaults.
Model backend is independent of data retrieval: fetching solicitations, literature,
and publication records happens over the network regardless of which model does the
reasoning.

name: claude-memory-backup
readme_excerpt:
# claude-memory-backup

An off-machine, versioned backup of Claude Code's per-project structured memory.

## Why this exists

Claude Code writes a small, curated memory for each project under
`~/.claude/projects/<encoded-project-path>/memory/`. Over time these notes
accumulate the things a repository does *not* preserve: which approaches were tried
and rejected and why, architecture rationale, results, and generalizable lessons. A
code repo shows the surviving final state; the memory dir is the record of how you
got there.

That memory lives in exactly one place — the `~/.claude` directory on a single
machine. It is not inside any project repo, so a normal `git push` of your projects
does not back it up, and a disk failure would lose it. This repository is the durable
copy and its version history.

It is intentionally **separate** from the code that produces it:

- **Scope.** `~/.claude/projects/` is ~300 MB, almost entirely raw session
  transcripts (`*.jsonl`) that contain whatever was pasted into a session. The
  curated memory is under 1 MB of it. This repo holds only the memory.
- **Sensitivity.** Transcripts can contain secrets and large pasted content. Keeping
  them out removes that exposure. This repo is private regardless.
- **Lifecycle.** Memory is data with a different churn and sensitivity profile than
  the tooling that maintains it. The sync script and hook live in the separate
  `aarons-harness` repo, not here.

## What is and isn't backed up

Backed up: every `*/memory/` directory under `~/.claude/projects/`, as Markdown.

Not backed up: session transcripts (`*.jsonl`), todo/tool state, anything else under
`~/.claude/`. The sync only ever reads from `*/memory/` directories.

## Layout

The repo mirrors the source tree:

```
<encoded-project-path>/memory/MEMORY.md
<encoded-project-path>/memory/<one fact per file>.md
```

For example, `~/.claude/projects/-Users-ads7fg-git-SchroederTrader/memory/` is
backed up to `-Users-ads7fg-git-SchroederTrader/memo

# STDN Explorer

Interactive dashboard for exploring **Shallow Technology Dependency Networks** (STDNs) — 4-layer directed acyclic graphs that map how technologies depend on components, raw materials, and producing countries.

Built as a companion tool for the technical report: *"From Technologies to Vulnerabilities: Multi-Agent Construction of Shallow Technology Dependency Networks for Supply Chain Risk Analysis"*.

**New to the dashboard?** See the [User Guide for Policy Analysts](docs/STDN_Explorer_User_Guide.md) or watch the [video walkthrough](https://github.com/dads2busy/stdn-explorer/releases/download/v1.0.0/stdn_explorer_walkthrough.mp4), which walk through every section using a concrete scenario: tracing the technologies that depend on Helium and assessing the impact of a reduction in Qatar's Helium production.

## What is an STDN?

An STDN captures the supply chain structure of a technology as a 4-layer DAG:

```
Technology → Components → Materials → Countries
```

For example, a **Smartphone** depends on a *Display Module*, which requires *Indium* (for ITO transparent conductors), which is primarily produced by *China* (57%), *South Korea* (15%), and *Japan* (10%).

## Domains

The explorer covers three technology domains, each with 60 products:

| Domain | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Microelectronics** | Smartphone, Data Center Server, MRI Machine, CubeSat On-Board Computer |
| **Biotechnology** | Real-Time PCR Thermocycler, Cryo-Electron Microscope, Viral Vector Production Bioreactor |
| **Pharmaceuticals** | Rotary Tablet Press, Aseptic Vial Filling Line, Medical Cyclotron |

A **Domain selector** in the header lets you switch between domains or view all 180 technologies combined. Each domain has its own set of technologies, components, materials, and country dependencies.

![Domain selector](docs/screenshots/domain-selector.png)

description: Illustrated guide + reproducible Python pipeline for creating sub-county geographic datasets for local policy analysis (Arlington broadband × income → civic associations).
name: local-level-data-guide
paragraph: This repository packages a reproducible pipeline and illustrated guide for disaggregating census and broadband data from block groups down to civic association boundaries—a practical solution to the common policy analysis problem of working with data at misaligned geographic scales. The core technical contribution is a reusable workflow that redistributes aggregate counts (income, households, broadband test results) using area-weighted methods via the `sdc.redistribute` package, then derives intensive rates from the redistributed counts; the pipeline recently expanded to include a parcel-centroid-based alternative approach with built-in comparison analysis to help practitioners understand where methods diverge. The project is active and well-maintained (92 commits, last updated mid-2026), with a notably hybrid architecture: the primary pipeline runs in Python using Census API integration and automated figure generation, but redistributes through an R package (`sdc.redistribute`, published to CRAN) that Aaron also maintains, giving researchers the flexibility to run either language. The deliverables are concrete—cleaned CSV/GeoJSON outputs ready for downstream analysis, plus a full suite of publication-quality maps and bivariate visualizations—making this simultaneously a research artifact and practical toolkit for local policy teams working with Arlington County broadband and income data.

# Local-Level Data Guide — Pipeline

Reproducible Python pipeline behind the illustrated guide to creating
sub-county geographic datasets (Arlington County: broadband × income →
civic associations).

## Setup

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12 && uv sync
export CENSUS_API_KEY=your_key   # free: https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html
# or put CENSUS_API_KEY=your_key in a .env file (gitignored)
```

### R (optional)

The redistribution algebra is also available in R via the
[`sdc.redistribute`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sdc.redistribute)
package, which powers the parallel pipeline in `pipeline-r/`:

```r
# released package from CRAN:
install.packages("sdc.redistribute")
# or the development version from the repository:
# install.packages("pak"); pak::pak("dads2busy/sdc.redistribute")
```

Then run the R pipeline from the repository root with `Rscript pipeline-r/run.R`.

## Run

```bash
uv run python -m pipeline.run
```

Outputs land in `data/`:
- `civic_income.csv`, `civic_broadband.csv` — redistributed measures
- `civic_combined.geojson` — joined + derived metrics (ratio, bivariate class)
- `civic_income_parcels.csv` — parcel-centroid income redistribution via `pipeline.acquire_parcels` + `redistribute_income_parcels`
- `civic_income_comparison.geojson` — side-by-side comparison of area-weighted vs parcel-based estimates (`compare_methods`)

## Method

Counts (aggregate income, households, broadband tests) are redistributed
area-weighted with `sdc-redistribute`; intensive rates (mean income, mean
speed) are derived from count ratios. The guide now includes a second,
parcel-based approach that assigns block-group income to civic associations
using parcel centroids as a spatial proxy, with a comparison chapter showing
where the two methods agree and diverge. See `docs/superpowers/specs/`.

description: Offline, config-driven compliance reviewer for grant proposals: scores a draft against a YAML rubric using a local two-model Ollama ensemble plus a deterministic keyword pass, then merges results into a combined report (md/html/pdf).
name: proposal-reviewer
paragraph: proposal-reviewer is a locally-run compliance scoring tool for grant proposals that bypasses cloud APIs entirely by orchestrating an offline two-model Ollama ensemble alongside deterministic keyword matching against a YAML-defined rubric. The engine is proposal-agnostic—all domain-specific logic (scoring criteria, point allocations, section mappings, keyword lists, and model selection) lives in per-opportunity config files, allowing a single Python script to handle diverse funding mechanisms (the repo includes examples for CDC and DOE calls). It accepts multiple input formats (.docx, .pdf, .md, .tex, .txt) and produces merged reports in Markdown, HTML, or PDF via Pandoc and WeasyPrint/TeX rendering. The project is actively maintained (last commit June 2026) with a deliberate focus on iteration speed: researchers can review and revise proposals repeatedly without API costs or network latency. Notable choices include the config-driven architecture for reusability, the dual-model ensemble to reduce hallucination through disagreement scoring, and the deterministic keyword pass as a guardrail against model drift—practical decisions reflecting Aaron's experience building research tools that balance rigor with usability for real proposal workflows.
readme_excerpt:
# proposal-reviewer

Offline, config-driven compliance review for grant proposals. Runs a two-model
**local** ensemble (via [Ollama](https://ollama.com)) plus a deterministic keyword
pass against a proposal, scores it against a rubric defined in a YAML config, and
merges everything into a combined report (`.md` / `.html` / `.pdf`).

Nothing leaves the machine and it consumes no cloud/API usage — the whole point is
to run proposal reviews locally and repeatedly while you iterate on a draft.

## Why config-driven

The engine (`proposal_reviewer.py`) is proposal-agnostic. Everything specific to a
given funding opportunity — criteria, point caps, section map, keywords, model
picks — lives in a YAML file under `configs/`. One engine, one config per proposal.

## Install

    brew install ollama pandoc          # pdftotext comes via poppler: brew install poppler
    pip install pyyaml
    ollama pull gemma3:27b              # two DIFFERENT families; both ~27-32B run
    ollama pull qwen2.5:32b             # comfortably on a 64GB machine
    # PDF rendering needs a Unicode-capable engine, one of:
    pip install weasyprint              # or a TeX with xelatex (brew install --cask mactex-no-gui)

Requires Ollama >= 0.19 (MLX backend on Apple Silicon).

## Use

    # Validate a config against a proposal without running models:
    python proposal_reviewer.py PROPOSAL --config configs/cdc-ip-26-0102.yaml --dry-run

    # Full review:
    python proposal_reviewer.py PROPOSAL --config configs/cdc-ip-26-0102.yaml

    # Override models ad hoc:
    python proposal_reviewer.py PROPOSAL --config CONFIG --models llama3.3:70b qwen3.6:27b

`PROPOSAL` can be `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.md`, `.tex`, or `.txt`. Reports are written
next to the proposal file.

description: Redistribute attribute values between geographic areas (area-weighted and dasymetric), an sf-native R package
name: sdc.redistribute
paragraph: sdc.redistribute is an R package that solves the geographic data harmonization problem of reallocating attribute values across misaligned polygon boundaries—a common challenge when integrating datasets with different spatial definitions. The package provides two core redistribution methods: `redistribute_direct` uses area-weighted interpolation to apportion values based on polygon overlap, while `redistribute_parcels` employs dasymetric refinement using a point layer (such as parcel centroids) as a spatial intensity guide for more accurate allocation. Built as a native sf package, it integrates seamlessly with R's modern spatial ecosystem and handles both extensive and intensive variables. The repository appears actively maintained with continuous integration via GitHub Actions, though the modest commit history (20 commits) and small codebase (~18KB) suggest it's a focused, specialized tool rather than a large-scale project. The implementation reflects practical research needs—specifically supporting spatial statistical disclosure control workflows given the "sdc" namespace—while remaining general enough for standard geographic data redistribution tasks.

name: national_capital_region_data
paragraph: The National Capital Region Data Commons is an interactive Next.js dashboard that surfaces demographic, economic, health, housing, and infrastructure indicators across the DC metro area and surrounding Maryland and Virginia counties. It solves the problem of navigating fragmented regional data by providing a unified interface with choropleth maps, time-series visualizations, ranked tables, and shareable URL state across eight geographic levels (county down to human services region), plus an integrated Gemini-powered AI assistant for exploratory analysis. The project is active and well-maintained, deployed as a static GitHub Pages site with a deliberate separation-of-concerns architecture: upstream Python pipelines produce compressed wide-format CSVs, a TypeScript build script (`build-data.ts`) decompresses and transforms them into JSON lookups and GeoJSON, and the Next.js frontend (React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, React Leaflet 5, Plotly.js) consumes those artifacts. State management uses Zustand with localStorage persistence for UI state, React Context for data loading coordination, and Nuqs for URL-driven filtering. Built data is gitignored and regenerated in CI, keeping the repository lean while ensuring reproducibility. The codebase demonstrates strong engineering discipline: TypeScript strict mode, Vitest unit tests, Playwright e2e tests, and careful lazy-loading of map components to avoid SSR complications.

# National Capital Region Data Commons

An interactive Next.js dashboard for exploring demographic, economic, health, housing, and infrastructure indicators across the National Capital Region (Washington, DC and surrounding counties in Virginia and Maryland).

The dashboard renders choropleth maps, time-series plots, and ranked tables across multiple geographic levels (county, tract, block group, civic association, zip code, planning district, supervisor district, and human services region) with shareable URL state and an integrated AI assistant.

## Live site

Deployed to GitHub Pages at `/national_capital_region_data/`.

```
social-data-commons (Python pipelines)

   committed under dashboard_data/national_capital_region_data/
                      
copied to data/*.csv.xz in this repo
                      
scripts/build-data.ts (npm run build:data)
   decompresses + transforms to JSON lookups
   writes public/data/*.json + datapackage.json
   copies GeoJSON to public/geo/*.geojson
                      
Next.js static export (npm run build)
   reads public/data + public/geo
   outputs ./out/  GitHub Pages
```

Built data (`public/data/`, `public/geo/`) is gitignored and regenerated in CI.

name: Social-Data-Commons
paragraph: Social Data Commons is a unified Python-based data pipeline monorepo designed to ingest, standardize, and distribute datasets across multiple social impact domains (demographics, health, housing, broadband, business climate, and others). The repository solves the problem of maintaining consistent data workflows and output formats across disparate data sources by providing a shared core framework (`sdc-core`) that handles Census API access, geographic crosswalks, standardization, and distributed I/O, while each domain maintains its own topic-specific ingestion scripts organized in a consistent directory structure (code, original data, working intermediate files, and compressed distribution outputs). The project is active and uses `uv` for dependency management with `pandas` and `httpx` as primary data manipulation and API access libraries, ultimately producing standardized long-form compressed CSV files (`*.csv.xz`) for downstream consumption. # Social Data Commons (SDC)

Unified monorepo for Social Data Commons data pipelines. This repo contains domain-specific pipelines plus a shared Python core for ingesting, standardizing, and distributing datasets across multiple social impact domains.

## Purpose

- **Goal**: ingest, standardize, and distribute SDC datasets across domains (demographics, health, housing, etc.).
- **Primary runtime**: Python, with shared utilities in `packages/sdc-core/`.

description: Simulated graduate-student annotator for gold-standard component data
name: simgrad
paragraph: simgrad is a Python tool that automates the generation of gold-standard component annotations for technologies by simulating a graduate-student researcher querying Claude with web search enabled. It solves the practical problem of scaling manual annotation work—rather than having humans laboriously document primary components for each technology, the system prompts Claude under a naive-grad-student persona to search the web and produce cited component lists, following a strict output schema. The tool is actively maintained (last commit May 2026) and feeds into a larger agentic system (`dpi_stdn_agentic`) that expands component gold standards. The workflow enforces careful human oversight: users manually curate a technology list (proportionally sampled across microelectronics, pharma, and biotech), generate and hand-review specifications, then run a calibration phase on existing gold-standard technologies to validate quality thresholds before expanding to new domains. Notable technical choices include using Claude's native web_search tool rather than custom retrieval, requiring citations in the output schema for explainability, a gated workflow with sentinel files that prevent expansion until calibration passes, and comprehensive failure reporting that guides users toward remediation (prompt tuning, search budget increases, or domain exclusion). The tool uses `uv` for dependency management and includes live integration tests that hit the real Claude API for verification.
readme_excerpt:
# simgrad

Simulated graduate-student annotator for gold-standard component data. Produces primary-component lists for technologies by running Claude with native `web_search` under a naive-grad-student persona and a citation-required output schema.

Consumed by `~/git/dpi_stdn_agentic/` to expand its component gold standard.

## Quickstart

```bash
uv sync
uv run simgrad calibrate
uv run simgrad expand --techs data/tech_list_expansion.csv
```

See `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-19-simgrad-design.md` for full design.

## Workflow

1. Populate `data/tech_list_expansion.csv` with 11–16 technologies (one per line) drawn proportionally across microelectronics, pharma, biotech.
2. `uv run simgrad specs --input data/tech_list_expansion.csv` — produces `data/tech_specifications.csv`. **Open and review** each spec by hand.
3. `uv run simgrad calibrate` — runs sims on the 4 existing gold-std techs. Writes `output/calibration/calibration_report.json`. Exits nonzero unless thresholds pass; on pass, writes `output/calibration/calibration_pass.json` sentinel.
4. `uv run simgrad expand --techs data/tech_specifications.csv` — runs sims on expansion techs. Refuses to run unless the calibration sentinel exists.
5. Copy `output/goldstandard_simulated.csv` into `~/git/dpi_stdn_agentic/data/goldstndrd_simulated.csv` (or symlink). It does not replace `goldstndrd.csv`; both can be used by validation scripts.

If calibration fails, the report at `output/calibration/calibration_report.json` lists per-tech failures. Options: (a) tune prompts in `src/simgrad/prompts/grad_student.md`, (b) raise `SIMGRAD_MAX_SEARCHES`, (c) document the limitation and exclude that domain from expansion.

## Live integration test

```bash
SIMGRAD_LIVE=1 uv run pytest tests/test_integration_live.py -v
```

Hits the real Claude API; burns tokens. Useful to verify wiring after big changes.

# STDN Agentic Framework

A multi-agent AI system for generating **Shallow Technology Dependency Networks (STDNs)** through iterative debate, critique, and consensus-building.

## Overview

STDN Agentic automates the analysis of global technology supply chains by orchestrating LLM-powered agents that propose, critique, and refine technology dependency networks. The framework maps:

```
Technologies → Components → Materials → Producing Countries
```

Each link includes confidence scores and reasoning, making the analysis auditable and interpretable.

## Architecture

The system uses a four-stage pipeline with optional multi-agent debate in Stages 1–3:

```
┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐

│ Component Extraction │ Materials Mapping    │ Country Data         │ Post-Processing Norm.  │
├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
│ • N debating agents  │ • N debating agents  │ • USGS Database      │ • Batch normalization  │
│ • Jaccard-based      │ • Jaccard-based      │ • LLM fallback       │ • Canonical vocab      │
│   convergence        │   convergence        │ • Voting/consensus   │ • JSON output          │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘
```

name: dpi_budget_estimation_agentic
paragraph: This repository implements a multi-agent LangGraph workflow to estimate classified U.S. intelligence spending by reconciling public budget documents against disclosed aggregate totals. The system addresses a transparency problem: while the government publishes high-level National Intelligence Program (NIP) and Military Intelligence Program (MIP) figures, detailed breakdowns remain classified. By systematically identifying observable line items in public documents and attributing the residual gap to classified programs, the project operationalizes a top-down reconciliation methodology as a repeatable, auditable pipeline. The architecture decomposes budget estimation into clearly-defined agent stages using Pydantic AI with typed state, implementing a Shallow Technology Dependency Network where each node has explicit inputs, outputs, and dependencies. This design enables analysts to understand the inference process, audit intermediate results, and extend the workflow across fiscal years and scenarios. The codebase is actively maintained (64 commits, last update April 2026) and mixes Python (primary implementation), JavaScript, and Shell scripting. The multi-agent approach trades monolithic script simplicity for modularity and explainability—critical for policy-relevant work where stakeholders need to understand how residual estimates were derived from public data and disclosed totals.
readme_excerpt:
# Intelligence Budget Estimation System

The Intelligence Budget Estimation System is a multi-agent, LangGraph-based workflow that estimates the classified portion of U.S. intelligence spending by reconciling public budget documents against disclosed national and military intelligence program totals. Instead of treating this as a single monolithic script, the project is structured as a set of collaborating agents and workflow nodes that implement a Shallow Technology Dependency Network for budget estimation: each step has clearly defined inputs, outputs, and dependencies, and each is implemented as a Pydantic AI agent with typed state. This README provides a narrative tour of the problem, the architecture, and the codebase so that analysts, researchers, and multi-agent engineers can understand both the methodology and how to extend it.

---

## Problem and objectives

At its core, the system tackles a transparency problem: the U.S. government publishes high-level intelligence budget aggregates (NIP and MIP) but does not provide a detailed public breakdown of where those funds go. The objective of this project is to infer the “black budget” residual by systematically identifying all observable line items in public documents, reconciling them against the published totals, and attributing the remaining gap to classified programs. The application operationalizes the top-down reconciliation methodology using AI agents so that the process is repeatable, auditable, and extensible across fiscal years.

Conceptually, the system implements the following relationship across multiple years and scenarios:

\[
\text{Black Budget Residual} = (\text{NIP} + \text{MIP}) - (\text{Identified Accounts} - \text{Deduplication} + \text{Reprogramming})
\]

Rather than manually sourcing data, performing ad hoc classification, and hand-adjusting totals, the workflow encodes each of these conceptual terms as a stage in a multi-agent pipeline. Every stage is backed by structured Pydantic models

The repository maintains an authoritative manifest with MD5 checksums for all distributed files, enabling reproducible downstream analyses and reliable data lineage tracking. As of August 2022, the project appears dormant with 54 commits focused on curating geographies across multiple jurisdictions (DC, Maryland, Virginia). The approach reflects research data management best practices by separating raw inputs from processed outputs while keeping transformation logic transparent and version-controlled, making it a foundational infrastructure component for a data commons rather than a statistical or modeling tool.

name: TheRegistry2
paragraph: TheRegistry2 is an extensible ASP.NET Identity 2.0 project template designed to simplify customization of core identity models without wrestling with generic type parameters. The repository addresses a genuine friction point in the Identity framework: while extending the basic ApplicationUser class was manageable, extending Role implementations required substantial boilerplate. This template eliminates that friction by allowing developers to directly add properties and methods to Identity model classes defined in IdentityModels.cs, streamlining the customization workflow. The codebase is dormant (last activity June 2016, minimal commit history), but represents a focused educational artifact from the mid-2010s ASP.NET ecosystem. Notable technical choices include using string keys for identity models rather than integers (with a companion repository available for integer-key variants), and the project includes substantial accompanying blog posts explaining the underlying generic type mechanics. The mix of JavaScript, C#, HTML, and CSS suggests a full-stack MVC application, though the primary contribution is the C# identity infrastructure pattern. While dated relative to modern ASP.NET Core identity patterns, the repository served as a reference implementation addressing real pain points in ASP.NET Identity 2.0 extensibility during its era.
readme_excerpt:
AspNet Identity 2.0 Extensible Project Template
===============================================
This project expands upon the work done by the ASP.NET Identity Team in the Identity Samples project. The goal is to provide a basic project template wherein the core identity Model classes are easily extensible without messing about with the generic type arguments.

While extending the basic `ApplicationUser` class provided in the original Identity Samples project was always relatively straightforward, Extending the Role implementation required some significant work. 

In this project, you can simply add additional properties and/or methods to any of the Identity Model classes as defined in the IdentityModels.cs file. 

For more information, see:

* [ASP.NET MVC and Identity 2.0: Understanding the Basics](http://typecastexception.com/post/2014/04/20/ASPNET-MVC-and-Identity-20-Understanding-the-Basics.aspx)

* [ASP.NET Identity 2.0: Customizing Users and Roles](http://typecastexception.com/post/2014/06/22/ASPNET-Identity-20-Customizing-Users-and-Roles.aspx)

The code in this repo is for a project where the Identity models use string keys. If you prefer integer keys (and database PK fields) see this repo instead:

[AspNet Identity 2.0 Extensible Project Template (integer keys)](https://github.com/TypecastException/AspNet-Identity-2-With-Integer-Keys)

There is a lot of good information here about how things work under the hood with the generic types, even if you don;t plan to use the integer keys:
* [ASP.NET Identity 2.0 Extending Identity Models and Using Integer Keys Instead of Strings](http://typecastexception.com/post/2014/07/13/ASPNET-Identity-20-Extending-Identity-Models-and-Using-Integer-Keys-Instead-of-Strings.aspx)

Please feel free to open issues, report bugs, and/or shoot me a pull request if you see potential fixes/improvements.
